hints: Look closely at the DNA bases around arrow B. The sequence there is A C T, so ask yourself what would happen if a new T was pushed in between those bases.
Remember mRNA is complementary to the DNA template strand, so to get mRNA UAG you need DNA A T C. A pairs with U, T pairs with A, C pairs with G.
walkthrough:
**Work out what DNA sequence makes the stop codon**

The strand shown is the template strand, so mRNA is made by complementary base pairing, not by copying exactly.

To make mRNA UAG you need DNA ATC:
$$A \rightarrow U, T \rightarrow A, C \rightarrow G$$

**Look for where a T insertion can create ATC**

Read the DNA left to right: T C C A C T C G A T G C.

Around position B you have A C T. If you insert a T between the A and the C, you get A T C T. The first three bases are now ATC.

**Check the effect on translation**

That new ATC in the template will be transcribed into UAG in mRNA.

UAG is a stop codon, so translation will terminate early. No other insertion position creates ATC, so B is the answer.

options.A: Inserting T at the very start gives TTC C..., which transcribes to AAG..., not UAG, so no stop codon is formed.
options.B: Inserting T between A and C changes ACT to ATCT, creating ATC in DNA which transcribes to UAG stop codon in mRNA.
options.C: Inserting T here does not create an ATC triplet in the template, so the mRNA will not contain UAG at that point.
options.D: Inserting T here disrupts the CGA TGC region but does not produce ATC, so no UAG stop codon appears.
